Title: Modulation of Co spin state at Co3O4 crystalline-amorphous interfaces for CO oxidation and N2O decomposition

Modulation of Co spin state at Co3O4
crystalline-amorphous interfaces for
CO oxidation and N2O decomposition
Yunpeng Long, Xiao Zhu, Chuan Gao, Wenzhe Si, Junhua Li
& Yue Peng
Modulation of electronic spin states in cobalt-based catalysts is an effective
strategy for molecule activations. Crystalline-amorphous interfaces often
exhibit unique catalytic properties due to disruptions of long-range order and
alterations in electronic structure. However, the mechanisms of molecule
activation and spin states at interfaces remain elusive. Herein, we present a
Co3O4 spinel-based catalyst featuring crystalline-amorphous interfaces.
Characterization analyses conﬁrm that tetrahedral Co2+ is selectively etched
from bulk spinel, forming amorphous CoO islands on the surface. The resul-
tant symmetry breaking in the coordination ﬁeld induces a reconstruction of
the Co3+ 3 d orbitals, leading to high-spin states. In CO oxidation, the interface
serves as novel active sites with a lower energy barrier, facilitated by lattice
oxygen activation. In N2O decomposition, the interface promotes reassocia-
tion of dissociated oxygen through quantum spin exchange interactions. This
work provides a straightforward approach to modulating the spin state of
interfaces and elucidates their role in molecule activations.
As the global community advances toward carbon neutrality, the
adoption of ammonia as a sustainable energy source is gaining trac-
tion, particularly for its potential to signiﬁcantly reduce CO2 emissions
in sectors such as maritime and heavy-duty transportation1. However,
the combustion of ammonia in combination with conventional fuels
like gasoline or diesel, as seen in ammonia-fueled marine engines,
often leads to elevated emissions of pollutants, including N2O and CO2.
Moreover, given the high global warming potential (ca. 298 times that
of CO2) and its considerable ozone depletion potential3, Euro VII
emission regulations have recently incorporated an emission control
standard for N2O emissions. Consequently, developing innovative
aftertreatment processes for internal combustion engines to effec-
tively manage N2O emissions has become imperative. Rhodium-based
catalysts demonstrate promising N2O decomposition activity, but
their practical application is constrained by economic, thermal stabi-
lity, and sensitivity to ﬂue gas components such as O2 and H2O con-
centrations. Iron series metal oxides, such as Co-, Fe-, and Ni-based
oxides, have relatively small crystal ﬁeld splitting energy, making it
easy to form open-shell structures4,5. Moreover, they can also create
complex potential energy surfaces by spin transitions, promoting
surface
defects
and
homogeneous/heterogeneous
interfaces
to
become more active6,7. Therefore, it is of great signiﬁcance to design
appropriate surface or interface structures by electronic structure
control to meet speciﬁc reactions.
The interfaces between crystalline and amorphous metal oxides
(MnOx/LaMnO3, CoOx/Co3O4, etc.) are of interest due to their unsa-
turated coordination environments and defect-rich sites, endowing
them with improved reaction rates and selectivity8–12. These features
make them highly effective for various catalytic applications, lever-
aging the beneﬁts of both crystalline order and amorphous disorder to
optimize activity and stability. However, the identiﬁcation and
description of the interfaces still face challenges from characterization
technical and in-situ spectroscopic methods. First, the amorphous
surface is sensitive to temperatures, pressures and gas atmospheres.
Some technologies such as Raman spectroscopy or temperature pro-
grammed experiments could damage the amorphous structure, giving
rise to unreliable results9,13–16. Moreover, the crystallinity of crystalline-
amorphous interfaces is often poor, making the morphology vague or
even invisible. This also makes real-time in-situ monitoring during the
reaction process and establishing reaction pathways more difﬁcult.

Manipulation of spin polarization could tune the interaction
between d-orbital electrons and adsorbates through quantum
spin exchange interactions (QSEI), which modulate charge trans-
fer at the interface and energy barrier of the reaction18–21. For
instance, the N2O decomposition is inherently kinetically difﬁcult
due to spin-forbidden nature. That is, the reactant N2O exists in a
singlet state with all electrons paired. However, the product O2 is
in a triplet state, with two electrons occupying the frontier π*
orbitals that are aligned in parallel22. The singlet state of oxygen is
reported at an energy level of at least ~1.0 eV higher than the
triplet state. Thus, the magnetic properties of the crystalline-
amorphous interfaces, related to the spin polarization, emerge as
an important factor affecting kinetics of N2O decomposition.
Ideally, not only new interfacial sites can be introduced, but also
the symmetry of crystal coordination ﬁeld will be disturbed and
the spin state of the reaction sites can be changed.
Herein, we reported a simple strategy to yield the crystalline-
amorphous interface on Co3O4 spinel via alkali solution treatment
and calcinated at 550 °C for 4 h. The interface structure is described
using X-ray absorption ﬁne structure (XAFS), electron energy loss
spectroscopy (EELS) and soft X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS),
etc., and its dynamic evolutions in CO oxidation and N2O decom-
position are studied using in-situ diffuse reﬂectance infrared Fourier
transform spectroscopy (DRIFTS), in-situ near ambient pressure
X-ray
photoelectron
spectroscopy
(NAP-XPS)
and
O
isotope
exchange experiments. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations
are also employed to conﬁrm the spin states of Co and reaction
pathways. Our work clearly disentangles the spin state regulation
mechanisms on the crystalline-amorphous interfaces and demon-
strates their immense potentials in activation and reassociation of
oxygen at interface.
Results
Bulk structure and coordination conﬁguration
It is well-known that Co2+ ions in spinel (AB2O4) tetrahedron A site
easily migrate to surface from the bulk structure, forming a char-
acteristic surface Co2+ enrichment region (CoO, Co(OH)2, etc.).
Meanwhile, the octahedral Co3+ demonstrates enhanced structural
stability23,24. Co3O4 spinel was synthesized via precipitation method,
and subsequently etched using a series of KOH alkali solutions of
varying concentrations, leading to a partial leaching of Co2+ from the
bulk phase to the surface. The resultant samples were denoted as
Co3O4-ATx, where x represents the alkali concentration (1.0, 5.0,
10.0 mol/L). X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns (Supplementary Fig. S1)
illustrate that all the samples present cubic spinel structure (space
group Fd–3m). However, notable shifts (0.2 °) in the diffraction peaks
of Co3O4-ATx signify extensive lattice distortion after alkali etching.
The Raman bands (Fig. 1a) at 481, 522, and 620 cm–1 can be indicated to
the E2g, F2
2g, and F2g phonon modes of typically Co3O4, respectively25.
The band at 196 cm–1 corresponds to F1
2g symmetry of tetrahedral sites
(CoO4), which can be attributed to vibrational mode of Co2+–O2–. The
band at 690 cm–1 corresponds to A1g symmetry of octahedral sites
(CoO6), which can be attributed to vibrational mode of Co3+–O2–. The
blue shifts of bands on the Co3O4-AT5 conﬁrm the lattice distortion.
XRD Rietveld reﬁnement analysis (Fig. 1b and Supplementary
Table S1–S2) were further performed to investigate the crystal-
lographic structure. The reﬁnement results indicate a lattice distortion
resulting from alkali treatment, with the lattice parameters decreasing
from 8.088 Å to 8.086 Å. Furthermore, the atomic occupancy factor of
tetrahedral Co2+ decreases from 1.0 to 0.876, further substantiating the
migration of Co2+ from bulk to surface. These quantitative changes in
parameters encapsulate the structural alterations post-alkali etching.
The high-angle annular dark-ﬁeld scanning transmission electron
microscopy (HAADF-STEM) are shown in Fig. 1c. The Co3O4 spinel is
well crystallized, with predominantly exposed (110) crystal faces. After
alkali etching, amorphous phases and low-crystallized regions appear

The pre-edges of the Co3O4 spinel show peaks at ca. 7710 eV, which
originates from the transition from the 1 s core level to Co 3 d states

The pre-edge of Co3O4-AT5 is even weaker than that of the Co3O4
spinel sample. The results indicate that the structural symmetry is
partially damaged by the alkali solution etching. As known, owing to
the absence of spatial inversion symmetry of the tetrahedral Co2+, the
pre-edge peak exhibits enhanced electronic leaping30,31. Thus, the
reduction in the intensity of the pre-edge peak after alkali treatment
reafﬁrms a decline of the tetrahedral Co2+, which show good accor-

Surface electronic structure and local environment
To investigate the inﬂuence of alkali solution etching on catalyst sur-
face and lattice distortion, the Co L2,3-edge soft XAS (Fig. 2a) was
conducted, and the peaks at 778.0 and 793.0 eV can be attributed to
the electron transition from 2p3/2 and 2p1/2 to 3 d orbitals, respectively.
The decrease of L3/L2 ratio on the Co3O4-AT5 suggests that the valence
states of surface Co is lower than that on the Co3O4 spinel. Moreover,
the L3 peak splits into two separate peaks on the Co3O4-AT5. The ﬁrst
peak (1) symbolizes the t2g orbitals in Co 3 d, while the second peak (2)
is associated with the eg orbitals35. The intensity of the peak 2 on the
Co3O4-AT5 is signiﬁcantly lower than that for Co3O4, which suggests
that the electron transfer between the two phases alters the position of
eg orbitals within Co 3 d. Co 2p XPS are conducted to further evaluate
the valence state of surface Co (Fig. 2b). The Co 2p peaks of Co3O4-
AT5 shift to lower binding energies (779.69 to 778.80 eV), indicating
that the electron transfer is promoted, leading to the electron redis-
tribution of surface Co. The surface Co2+/Co3+ ratio (1.95) on the Co3O4-
AT5 is also higher than that on the Co3O4 (0.67, Supplementary
Table S4), which show good accordance with the Co L2,3-edge results.
Considering that the bulk results indicate a higher oxidation state of
Co on the Co3O4-AT5, whereas the surface results show the opposite
trend, we can reasonably infer that a certain proportion of low-valence
Co (Co2+) must be present on the surface of Co3O4-AT5 to balance the
charge.

between Co 3 d and O 2p, which correspond to the t2g and eg orbits,

The electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) is performed to
obtain localized chemical states of the Co3O4-AT5 surface. The annular
dark-ﬁeld images and the corresponding Co L2,3-edge and O K-edge
spectra are shown in Fig. 2d-f and Supplementary Fig. S11-S12. From the
image, the localized blurring of lattice fringes is clearly visible in an
irregular shape, indicating the possible presence of some amorphous
oxide states on the surface. Then we obtain a series of spectra across
this amorphous region (from point 1 to point 10 in Fig. 2d). The L3 and
L2 lines of Co L-edge are the transitions from 2p3/2 to 3 d and from 2p1/2
to 3 d, respectively, and their intensities can be related to the unoc-
cupied states of surface Co in 3 d orbitals, which can be used as valence
ﬁngerprints41. As for the O K-edge, the peaks labeled as a and b arise
from electron transition from O 1 s →2p states hybridized with Co
unoccupied 3 d, 4sp orbitals, respectively. Therefore, the Co oxidation
state can be discriminated by the relative intensities and energies of
peaks a and b. The EELS Co L2,3-edge and O K-edge results suggest that
the average valence state of surface Co on the amorphous region is
signiﬁcantly lower than that on the crystalline surface. And the Co-O
bond on the amorphous region is longer than that on the crystalline
surface.
Additionally, the surface Co-O bonds are also determined to be
weaker covalent and stronger ionic, and new sub-surface phases
emerge after electron beam irradiation (Supplementary Fig. S13),
which are attributed to the reaction of the electron beam on the oxy-
gen anions, especially those with low coordination at the surface,
further leading to the formationof oxygen vacancies and the reduction
of Co3+ to Co2+, highlighting the high activity of surface Co-O bonds.
Within the amorphous region, the average ratios of O K-edge Ia/Ib are
lower than those of crystalline region and the shift of O K-edge re-
emphasizes that the Co-O bonds within amorphous region are more
ionic and less covalent. Combined with the results of XPS and XANES,
the amorphous region is the undissolved CoO. According to the
Sabatier principle, the crystalline (Co3O4) -amorphous (CoO) interface
enhance the electron transfer and lattice oxygen activation via chan-
ging spin states and orbital hybridization, which is expected to be
more effective in oxygenated-containing catalytic reactions, such as
CO oxidation and N2O decomposition.
Catalytic performance and active site evolution
To explore the interfacial of the crystalline-amorphous interface cat-
alyst in ammonia-doped fueled vehicle exhaust emission control of gas
molecules such as CO and N2O, we ﬁrst evaluated the CO oxidation
performances of the catalysts, which is also a probe model for inves-
tigating the activity of lattice oxygen activity. As displayed in Fig. 3a,
the Co3O4-AT5 exhibits lower T50 and T90 values (170.8 and 216.3 °C,
respectively) compared to the spinel Co3O4 (225.4 and 273.4 °C).
Additionally, both Co3O4 and Co3O4-AT5 show stable activity for sev-
eral cycles (Supplementary Fig. S14a). As reported by literatures42, the
CO oxidation on Co3O4 primarily follows the Mars-van-Krevelen (MvK)
mechanism, wherein lattice oxygen participates in the oxidation pro-
cess, while gas-phase oxygen replenishes the catalyst by reﬁlling oxy-
gen vacancies. Our CO/O2/N2 switching cycle tests also conﬁrmed that
CO oxidation over the Co3O4 and Co3O4-AT5 catalysts adheres to the
MvK mechanism (Supplementary Fig. S15). However, the reduction
peaks of lattice oxygen (transitioning from Co3+ to Co2+ and Co2+ to
Co0), which remain largely unaffected in the temperature programmed
reduction of CO (CO-TPR, Fig. 3b), convey that the activity of lattice
oxygen is nearly uniform. Therefore, the signiﬁcantly enhanced CO
conversions of Co3O4-AT5 can be attributed to its superior ability to
dissociate oxygen to replenish lattice oxygen. In validation of this
point, we likewise executed 18O-16O isotope exchange experiments. As
shown in the 18O2 isothermal isotope exchange results (Supplementary
Fig. S16a, b), the Co3O4 spinel displays a perceptible 18O16O signal
above 550 °C, conversely, the Co3O4-AT5 exhibits an explicit 18O16O
signal at 340 °C and a more robust 18O16O signal beyond 521 °C than
Co3O4. These collective ﬁndings afﬁrm the optimal oxygen dissocia-
tion and mobile recombination capacity of Co3O4-AT5. However,
homo-exchange (i.e., exchange between gaseous O2 molecules) can-
not be observed in
18O2 isothermal isotope exchange, only the
exchange between gaseous O2 and surface lattice oxygen can be
demonstrated. Hence, 16O2:18O2 = 1:1 isotope exchange (Supplementary
Fig. S16c, d) was further conducted to determine the levels of catalytic
activity toward the dissociation of oxygen17. Under the presence of
both 16O2 and 18O2, the Co3O4-AT5 also exhibits a much low tempera-
ture (265 °C) of 18O16O signal than that of Co3O4 (330 °C), reconﬁrming
its excellent O2 dissociation and O recombination properties.
Temperature programmed reduction of H2 (H2-TPR) is further
employed to investigate the interfacial properties (Supplementary
Fig. S17a). The reduction temperature of Co3O4-AT5 (350.7 °C) is
notably lower than that of the Co3O4 spinel (383.7 °C), implying that
the amorphous region enhances the reduction of crystalline Co3O4 in
H2. Promotion of Co3+/Co2+ reduction in Co3O4-AT5 by H2 but not by
CO can be closely related to H2 dissociation in the interface. The sig-
niﬁcant difference in selectivity of typical CO2 hydrogenations con-
ﬁrms the unique reduction property of the crystalline-amorphous
interface (Supplementary Fig. S17b). The products of Co3O4 spinel
predominantly comprises CH4 (90.4%) and a nominal quantity of CO.
Conversely, the Co3O4-AT5 displays a reduction in CO2 conversion but
manifests a signiﬁcant alteration in product distribution. Speciﬁcally,
CO selectivity signiﬁcantly increases from 9.6% to 85.2%, while CH4
selectivity decreases from 90.4% to 14.8%. In-situ NAP–XPS is further
performed to study the hydrogen spillover effect (Supplementary
Fig. S18).With increasing the temperature, the Co3O4-AT5 is facileto be
reduced compared to the Co3O4 spinel. Moreover, during the reduc-
tion process in 1.0 mbar CO2 + H2 (1:3) at 300 °C, Co3+ can be gradually
reduced to Co2+ and then further to Co0. It is observable that the Co2+

Mechanism for CO oxidation and N2O decomposition
DFT + U calculations (Ueff = 4.0 eV for Co) were then performed to
elucidate
the
electron
transfer
mechanism
at
the
crystalline-
amorphous interface and its role in catalytic reactions. The Co3O4
(110) and Co3O4-AT5 (110) models are shown in Supplementary
Fig. S22. The amorphous conﬁguration with the global minimum
energy is obtained using ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simu-
lations via the melting and annealing processes, which has been
proved to be reliable in theoretical calculation43–45. The local distortion
strain effect induced by the crystalline-amorphous interface enables
d–d electron transfer and p–π conjugation over medium and long
distances, thereby facilitating charge transfer between the crystalline
and amorphous regions46,47. As visualized by the differential charge
density (Fig. 4a), an obvious electron rearrangement is discernible,
suggesting an active electronic interaction between modeled crystal-
line and amorphous regions. This interaction results in a greater
transfer of electrons from the amorphous to the crystalline substrate.
To gain more insight into the electronic structure of the interface,
electron localization function (ELF), electron spin density, total density
of states (TDOS), projected density of states (PDOS) and crystal orbital
Hamilton population (COHP) of the models are calculated (Supple-
mentary Fig. S23). ELF results indicate that the electrons are almost
localized around O, forming Co-O ionic bonds. Moreover, the Co-O
bonds of Co3O4-AT5 (110) model is more ionic, which is consistent with
EELS and XAS results. The electron spin densities of the Co3O4 (110)
and Co3O4-AT5 (110) models are shown in Fig. 4b, c. In the Co3O4 (110)
model, the tetrahedral Co2+ cations are in high-spin states. However,
due to asymmetry, partial octahedral Co3+ cations in the ﬁrst layer also
exhibit high-spin states, while others below the second layer are in low-
spin states. In the Co3O4-AT5 model, all octahedral Co3+ cations are in
high-spin states. The average magnetic moments of Co2+ and Co3+ of
Co3O4 (110) model are 2.54 ± 0.47 and 0.21 ± 0.40 μB, while those for
the Co3O4-AT5 model are 2.23 ± 0.72 and 2.38 ± 0.25 μB (Supplemen-
tary Table S5), respectively. This is consistent with the electronic
analysis by XAS spectra, which indicates that lattice distortion caused
by the formation of the crystalline-amorphous interface facilitates the
spin mutation of Co3+ from low-spin to high-spin states. TDOS and
PDOS (Fig. 4d, e) results show an interstitial state between valence
band and conduction band of the Co3O4-AT5 (110) model and the
d-band center shifts from -2.72 to -2.55 eV. This change can promote
the electron transfer process in the reaction and the adsorption
strength of gas molecules. COHP are then calculated to further
investigate bonding characteristics, focusing on the bonding and
antibonding interactions (Supplementary Fig. S24). The COHP analysis
provides a critical insight: the integrated—ICOHP values for the Co2+-O
and Co3+-O bonds in the Co3O4-AT5 (110) model are 0.62 and 0.70,
respectively, which are lower than the 1.61 and 1.67 calculated in the
Co3O4 (110) model. The results indicate that the Co-O bonds in the
Co3O4-AT5 (110) model are weaker than those in the Co3O4 (110)
model, making them more prone to defect formation and more likely
to participate in CO oxidation.
Given the CO oxidation and N2O decomposition reactions occur
at high temperatures and the entropy contribution cannot be neglec-
ted, we calculated the free energy proﬁles for different reaction tem-
peratures (Supplementary Figs. S25, S26). From the thermodynamic
perspective on energy change proﬁles at 473 K, it was observed that
the CO displays a stronger adsorption on the Co3O4-AT5 (110) model
with the adsorption free energy at -0.28 eV (interfacial Co3+ site) than
Co3O4 (110) model (surface Co3+ site, -0.08 eV), consistent with the
d-band theory. The initial reaction from CO* to CO2 occurs at a rela-
tively lower energy barrier of 0.49 eV than the Co3O4 (110) model
(0.78 eV), owing to the more reactive surface-oxygen species.
According to the MvK mechanism, an O vacancy site is created upon
the formation of the ﬁrst CO2 molecule, further ﬁlled by the adsorption
of O2(g). For the Co3O4 (110) model, the free energy of O2(g) adsorp-
tion is 0.20 eV. The second CO oxidation step occurs with an energy
barrier lower (Ea = 0.43 eV) than the ﬁrst oxidation step, involving a
subsequently adsorbed CO bonding to an O atom of the adsorbed O2*.
The original Co3O4 (110) model is restored upon the desorption of the
second CO2*, thus completing the entire cycle. While in the Co3O4-AT5
(110) model, the free energy of O2(g) adsorption on O vacancy site is
-0.15 eV, much stronger than that on the Co3O4 (110) model. Addi-
tionally, the dissociated O* species can participate in the second CO
oxidation step by interfacial overﬂow onto the crystalline phase, with
an energy barrier at only 0.31 eV.
In the N2O decomposition, from the thermodynamic perspective
on energy change proﬁles at 673 K (Fig. 4g), N2O tends to be adsorbed
on the cobalt site on the Co3O4 (110) model in the form of
Co3+–N–N–O–Co2+ type. When N2O is chemically adsorbed on the Co
site, the N–O band is active to create the *O intermediate, and then N2
is desorbed. In the following steps, the two *O intermediates migrated
and formed into O2* molecules (corresponding to the Oβ species in
Fig. 3f) and desorbed from surface. In the Co3O4-AT5 (110) model, N2O
tends to adsorb onto the amorphous region in the form of
N–N–O–Co2+. The N2O adsorbed on the Co3O4-AT5 (110) model gains
more electrons compared to the Co3O4 (110) model, which is believed
to facilitate the activation of N2O (Supplementary Fig. S27). The free
energy proﬁle of the N2O decomposition pathway reveals that for the
Co3O4 (110) model, the migration of the *O species is the rate-
determining step, with a reaction energy barrier of 2.03 eV. However,
in the Co3O4-AT5 (110) model, the energy barrier for *O species
migration and recombination decreases to only 0.98 eV.
Our DFT calculations indicate that the high-spin Co3+ sites facil-
itate more efﬁcient adsorption and activation of gas molecules. Addi-
tionally, the crystalline-amorphous interface in the Co3O4-AT5 (110)
model enhances CO oxidation activity by providing a lower energy
pathway at the interface and high-spin Co3+ sites. Furthermore, this
interface also improves the migratory and reassociation of oxygen
species by quantum spin exchange interactions in the Co3O4-AT5 (110)
model, resulting in excellent performance in N2O decomposition.
Discussion
In summary, the crystalline-amorphous interface of Co3O4 catalyst is
prepared by alkali etching method, in which the crystalline region is
Co3+ cations in Co3O4 spinel lattice, and the amorphous region is CoO.
The abundance of defects disrupts the symmetry of the coordination
ﬁeld in octahedral crystals, causing the energy levels in Co 3 d orbitals
to split and leading to the transition of t2g electrons to eg orbitals. This
transition reconﬁgures octahedral Co from a low-spin to a high-spin
state. In comparison to the face-to-face t2g orbitals, the apex-to-apex eg
electron transfer mode has higher transfer efﬁciency and demon-
strates stronger adsorption and activation capabilities for reactant
molecules. In CO oxidation, the etched catalyst exhibits superior

magnetic oxygen-containing intermediate species to oxygen mole-

interactions, which enhances the N2O decomposition activity. This
investigation provides a new approach to catalyst design by integrat-
ing atomic-level crystalline/amorphous interfaces, offering a theore-

Methods
Materials
Cobaltous (II) nitrate hexahydrate (Co(NO3)2·6H2O, ≥99.0%), sodium
carbonate (Na2CO3, ≥99.8%) and potassium hydroxide (KOH, ≥85.0%)
purchased from Sinopharm, were used as received without further
puriﬁcation.
Catalyst preparation
(1) Synthesis of spinel Co3O4: The Co3O4 catalyst was prepared by
precipitation method. 116.4 g of Co(NO3)2·6H2O (0.4 mol) and 53.0 g of
Na2CO3 (0.5 mol) were dissolve in 250 mL of deionized water,
respectively. Then, mixed and stirred them in a water bath at 50 °C for
2 h. The precipitate was then ﬁltered and washed several times, dried
overnight at 80 °C, and ﬁnally calcined in a mufﬂe furnace at 550 °C for
4 h at a heating rate of 1 °C/min.
(2) Synthesis of Co3O4-ATx: The Co3O4-ATx catalyst was prepared
by etching spinel Co3O4 using a series of KOH alkali solutions of
varying concentrations (labeled as Co3O4-ATx, where x denotes alkali
concentration, 1.0, 5.0, 10.0 mol/L), resulting in crystalline-amorphous
interfaces. The etched precipitates were washed several times (to wash
away the residual K+ ions) before dried overnight at 80 °C, and ﬁnally
calcined in a mufﬂe furnace at 550 °C for 4 h at a heating rate of
1 °C/min.

Characterization
X-ray powder diffraction (XRD) patterns were obtained using a dif-
fractometer (D/max–2500, Rigaku, Japan) with Cu Kα radiation
(λ = 0.15418 nm) (2θ = 20 ° to 80 °, step of 0.1 °). X-ray photoelectron
spectroscopy (XPS) was conducted on a Thermo ESCALAB 250 spec-
trometer from VG Scientiﬁc with Al Kα radiation. All the binding
energies of the samples were calibrated to the C 1 s line at 284.8 eV.
Brunner–Emmet–Teller (BET) surface area and pore size distributions
were analyzed using a Micromeritics ASAP 2020 analyzing apparatus
(USA). Before N2 physisorption, samples were pretreated at 300 °C for
1 h under vacuum. The surface area was calculated using the N2 iso-
therm data and BET model. Raman spectra were obtained on a
Renishaw laser Raman spectrometer (RAMANLOG 6). The emission
beam at 532 nm from an Ar+ ion laser (Spectra Physics) was focused on
the sample under the microscope. The power of the incident beam on
the sample was below 10 mW (100 ~ 4000 cm-1). High angle ring dark
ﬁeld (HAADF) images were obtained on FEI Titan 80–300 ﬁeld emis-
sion spherical aberration corrected scanning transmission electron
microscope (STEM) with the energy resolution ≤0.7 eV.
Temperature-programmed reduction by H2 (H2-TPR) was con-
ducted on a Chemisorb 2920 chemical adsorption analyzer (Micro-
meritics, USA) equipped with a thermal conductivity detector (TCD).
The catalyst (0.05 g) with 40–60 mesh was pretreated in 5 vol.% O2/He
(30 mL min−1, 400 °C, 1 h). After purging with 6 vol.% H2/N2 (30 mL min−1,
100 °C, 1 h), the catalyst was heated to 900 °C at a rate of 10 °C/min. The
consumed H2 was recorded using a TCD. Temperature-programmed
desorption of O2 (O2-TPD) was carried out on a Chemisorb 2920 che-
mical adsorption analyzer (Micromeritics, USA). First, 0.1 g catalyst with
40–60 mesh was pretreated under a purge of 5 vol.% O2/He
(30 mL min−1, 400 °C, 1 h). After being purged with He (30 ml/min, 100
°C, 1 h), the catalyst was heated from 100–900 °C, and O2 desorption
was measured using a thermal conductivity detector. The electron
paramagnetic resonance (EPR) measurements were conducted using
the JEOL JES-FA 200 X-band ESR spectrometer. Singlet oxygen (1O2) in
the outlet gas was trapped by DMPO at a temperature of 20% N2O
conversion, and the reacted catalyst surface O2
−was captured
using TEMP.
The X-ray absorption spectra (XAS) including X-ray absorption
near-edge structure (XANES) and extended X-ray absorption ﬁne
structure (EXAFS) of the samples at the Co K-edge (7709 eV) were
collected at the XAFCA beamline of Singapore Synchrotron Light
Sources (SSLS) center, where a pair of channel-cut Si (111) crystals was
used in the monochromator. The storage ring was working at the
energy of 0.7 GeV with a below 200 mA for average electron current.
The Co K-edge XAS data were acquired in a transmission mode at room
temperature. The Co L-edge and O K-edge XAS spectra were recorded
at the SUV beamline of SSLS. Data acquisition was carried out in total
electron yield (TEY) mode with a photon energy resolution of 350 meV.
All obtained XAS data were processed and analyzed using the Demeter
software package48. Energy calibration, background removal, and
normalization was conducted using Athena (version 0.9.26) software.
Then Fourier transform and Fourier transformed ﬁtting of Co K-edge
was carried out in Athena (version 0.9.26) and Artemis (version
0.9.26). The k3 weighting, k-range of 2.39 ~ 10.85 Å−1 and R range of
1 ~ 3.54 Å were used for the ﬁtting of the Co K-edges. The continuous
Cauchy wavelet was used to wavelet transform the k3-weighted EXAFS
signals by a high-level programing language MATLAB R2020a-based
code49.
In-situ near-ambient pressure X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy
(in-situ NAP −XPS) measurements were performed on the SPECS
NAP −XPS system. All spectra are monochromatized Al Kα irradiation
(1486.6 eV) produced using an aluminum anode (SPECS XR −50), and
excitation source power ﬁxed at 50 W. Since the differential pumping
system separates the electronic analyzer (SPECS Phoibos NAP −150)
from the reaction zone, XPS measurements can be made at pressures
up to 25 mbar. The nozzle bore is 0.3 mm. The reaction pressure is
maintained at 1 mbar by a pressure reducing valve.
In-situ diffuse reﬂectance infrared Fourier transform (in-situ
DRIFT) spectroscopy was conducted on a Nicolet iS50 FT-IR spectro-
meter (Waltham, USA). The DRIFT cell was equipped with ZnSe win-
dows. The infrared spectrum was measured with scan of 32 and a
resolution of 4 cm–1 in the range of 400–800 cm–1. Prior to the tests,
the catalyst was pretreated in 50 mL·min–1 He (500 °C, 1 h), and then
naturally cooled to 300 °C. The background spectrum was collected at
300, 400, and 500 °C during the cooling process and was subtracted
from the sample spectra collected at the corresponding temperature.
Thereafter, 2000 ppm N2O/He (50 mL·min–1) was introduced into the
reaction cell, and the spectra were recorded for 30 min at 300, 400,
and 500 °C, respectively.
Catalytic performance measurements
The catalyst (100 mg) was placed on the packed-bed reactor. Before
activity evaluation, the catalyst was treated for 1 h under the con-
ditions of 300 °C and 100 mL·min–1 high-purity N2 gas ﬂow. During
the CO oxidation reaction, the gas ﬂow rate was 100 mL·min–1
([CO] = 1 vol%, [O2] = 21 vol%, N2 balance), and the weight hourly
space velocity (WHSV) was 60000 mL·g–1 · h–1. During the N2O
decomposition reaction, the gas ﬂow rate was 100 mL·min–1
([N2O] = 2000 ppm, [O2] = 5 vol.% (when used), [H2O] = 5 vol.%
(when used), N2 balance), and the weight hourly space velocity
(WHSV) was 60000 mL h−1 gcat
−1. Each reaction temperature point
shall be kept warm for 1 h. Use Fourier transform infrared con-
tinuous gas analyzer (GASMET DX −4000) to monitor the CO, CO2,
N2O, H2O concentration at the outlet online.
For CO2 hydrogenation reaction, the catalytic testing was carried
out in a U-tube ﬁxed-bed reactor at ambient pressure. The feed gas
consisted with 72 vol% H2, 24 vol% CO2 and 4 vol% Ar, and the weight
hourly space velocity (WHSV) was 30000 mL h−1 gcat
−1. The reactivity
was tested stepwise from 200 to 400 °C at 50 °C intervals, with a
duration of 60 min at each temperature. Products were analysed
online with an Agilent 7820 A gas chromatograph equipped with TDX-
01 and a 5 Å molecular sieve column and PEG-20M capillary column.
Gas products were examined with a thermal conductivity detector and
a ﬂame ionization detector.
DFT calculations
All the spin-polarized density functional theory (DFT) + U calculations
were performed within the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP
5.4.4) code50–55. The Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) functional in the
generalized gradient approximation (GGA) was employed to describe
the exchange–correlation functional56, and the project augmented
wave (PAW) method was used to describe the core-valence electron
interaction with an energy cutoff of 500 eV51,56. Partial occupancies of
the Kohn−Sham orbitals were allowed using the Gaussian smearing
method and a width of 0.05 eV. The vacuum between slabs was 15 Å to
avoid interactions between the neighboring slabs. The ﬁrst Brillouin
zone integration was generated by VASPKIT with a k-point mesh of
1 × 1 × 1 in the Γ-centered Monkhorst-Pack scheme57,58. The electronic
energy was considered self-consistent when the energy change was
<10−6 eV. For geometry optimization, the systems were relaxed until
the force reached the convergence threshold of 0.02 eV·Å−1. The van
der Waals interactions were taken into considered by the Grimme
(DFT + D3) method59,60. Moreover, a Hubbard-like term (Ueff = coulomb
U −exchange J) was applied for Co atoms, and the Ueff value was
4.0 eV61,62. To obtain the transition states and reaction pathway, the
transition state tools for VASP-VTST package with climbing image
nudged elastic band (CI-NEB) was used63,64. Given the process of CO
oxidation and N2O decomposition were carried out at the temperature
range of 373-573 and 473-773 K, respectively. The free energy was
calculated at different temperature using the equation: G = E + ZPE −

Crystal orbital Hamilton population (COHP) analysis was per-
formed with the LOBSTER 3.2.0 package, enabling the quantiﬁcation of
interatomic interactions and the estimation of quantum-chemical

atom-in-molecule scheme proposed by Bader66. The visualization of
models were analyzed by using the VESTA 3.5.8 code and Material

the VESTA code.
The ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulation was employed
to simulation the amorphous CoO by VASP code. To approach a realistic
amorphous structure, a canonical (NVT) ensemble with the Nose-Hoover
thermostat was applied to control the temperature and the pressure in
AIMD simulations. The initial system was melted and equilibrated at
2000 K for 10 ps to remove the possible memory effect from the initial
conﬁguration. Then, the temperature was decreased to 300 K, followed
by an equilibration time of 5 ps. After quenching, the resulting amor-
phous structure was subjected to geometry optimization to eliminate
residual stresses and unreasonable atomic distribution.
